items.title: GTA 6 Will Do Something the Franchise Has Never Done Before: Encourage Empathy
items.excerpt: Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 features something the franchise has never had before: mechanisms that encourage empathy.
items.content_text: Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 features something the franchise has never had before: mechanisms that encourage empathy. Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson and head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe talked about how next week's Grand Theft Auto changes the formula the series is known for during an interview with The Guardian (via @GameRoll_ ). Jason and Lucia will surely be able to cause a fair amount of chaos when players take control in Vice City, but in a post- Red Dead Redemption 2 world, they'll have the freedom to be kind, too. "Crime is a fundamental part of GTA – at least up until now, it has been," Nelson said. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." Games like GTA 5 have given players playgrounds and characters that can maximize the mayhem. Trevor, one of that game's three protagonists, is a great example of this chaotic energy, but in GTA 6, there doesn't seem to be a direct equivalent. Sure, Rockstar's trademark tone and instantly recognizable characters can be seen all over what few trailers we've received thus far, but everything seems a bit more grounded, too. Falling in line with this is the news that GTA 6 will feature a world that might actually reward those who take the citizens of Leonida into consideration. Of course, that doesn't mean those who prefer to wreak havoc won't be able to play their way, too. It just means that, at least based on Nelson's words, there's some room to be a normal or even good person, too. "I would say so," he replied when asked if the new game would encourage empathy in some capacity. "I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to." Elsewhere in the interview, Nelson described Jason and Lucia as a "younger couple with their backs against the wall," which is why it doesn't make sense for them to "go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can." This isn't Michael, Franklin, or Trevor, nor is it Niko Bellic. Thankfully, we won't have to wait too much longer to find out just what kind of criminals Jason and Lucia are, or who they can be. GTA 6 launches November 19, 2026, for PS5 and Xbox Series X | S. With more grounded in-game mechanisms and NPCs that react to weapons, it's clear we're staring down what will likely be the most realistic Grand Theft Auto game so far. It's something that has plenty of fans excited and others nervous . Recent footage shared by Rockstar has highlighted the game's unbelievable graphics . It's something that has IGN writer Jacqueline Thomas excited , even if it does run at 30 fps .
items.title_en: GTA 6 Will Do Something the Franchise Has Never Done Before: Encourage Empathy

items.title: Daggerheart: Hope & Fear Expansion Review
items.content_text: Critical Role’s TTRPG system, Daggerheart, puts a greater emphasis on story-telling than some of its peers. A year after the core book was released, Daggerheart offered players and Game Masters new options for telling their stories.with the system’s first expansion. As someone who plays a variety of role-playing games on both sides of the GM screen, I’m always hungry for more options. More gear for my heroes to use and more vicious monsters to sic on my unsuspecting players. Daggerheart: Hope and Fear adds a plethora of toys to the toybox, but if you weren’t a fan of the core book, don’t expect this expansion to change your mind. Before diving into what’s new, for those unfamiliar, Daggerheart is a narrative-focused tabletop RPG system. It uses a rather handy card-based approach to help create and manage your characters and does away with the traditional initiative mechanic during combat. One of the most defining mechanics of Daggerheart, however, is its Hope and Fear dice. These two twelve-sided dice, one representing your Hope value and the other Fear, can either cause your checks to earn you a 'Hope' resource that can be used to pull off extra special actions, or give your GM a 'Fear' point that they can spend. A proverbial "wrench in the gears" sort of treat, depending on which die rolls higher during the check. This mechanic also serves as the namesake for the system’s first expansion. Where to Buy The Daggerheart: Hope & Fear expansion is available to buy at the Critical Role shop for $39.99. For players who have been wanting to make some new characters, a plethora of options await you inside this nearly 200-page tome. The Hope and Fear expansion comes with four new classes, each with two subclasses, six ancestries and communities, over 100 new pieces of gear and loot to dig through, and a brand-new domain. GMs get some new toys too, with 130+ new enemies to sic on those pesky heroes across 28 environments and four campaign frames (think of these as rough bases to build a campaign around). By far, though, my personal favorite inclusion in H&F is the brand-new Transformations system, but more on that gem in a bit. The new domain, Dread, actually has some pretty interesting effects. The ones I found most intriguing and beneficial were abilities like Avatar of Terror, which makes you stronger the more Fear the GM has, and the spell Dire-Strike, which straight-up takes some of the GM’s Fear away. The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make. "The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make." Two new classes, the Assassin (a standalone, more stabby-focused rogue) and the Brawler (Daggerheart’s punchy monk-like class), utilize the core domains that came in the core book, while the other two new classes, the Warlock (make a pact with a thing, get cool powers) and the Witch (mess with enemies by hexing them), take advantage of H&F’s new Dread domain. The new ancestries, which for D&D folks are basically Daggerheart’s equivalent to species, will feel familiar to anyone who’s played that other high-fantasy TTRPG. The Aetheris are winged, angel-y beings, while Elemental Kin—consisting of Earth, Ember (fire), Sky, and Tide (water) varieties—are individuals descended from powerful elementals. And then you have Gnomes, which are, well, gnomes. All certainly good to have, but both the new ancestries and some of the new classes seem like such core fantasy staples that it feels odd to me that they weren’t included in the base release. Glad they’re here now, though, and gnomes being able to just teleport around with their Flicker Step feature is silly fun. For the forever Game Masters out there (you are the real heroes), Hope & Fear’s new campaign frames offer good flexibility for running games for hesitant brand-new players or grizzled vets that want a challenge. My favorite out of the four offerings, surprisingly, is also the least complex: Castle High. Think modern-day wizard school where teenagers fly around on brooms while scrolling on their phones and take classes on giant floating islands in the sky. While I haven’t yet played or run the frame, the idea of swapping out my sword for pencil and paper and sneaking out of school instead of dungeons is a fun change of pace. Of course, if you want to slay a dragon, or in this case a weredragon tyrant, you can do that too with Reign of the Weredragon. The most complex of the new offerings, Journey to Horizon, has you working to resurrect a goddess. Now we can get to my favorite addition: transformations. Becoming a demigod, a werewolf, a vampire, or even living out your Danny Phantom dreams by transforming into a ghost is now possible! All of the transformation options in H&F (of which there are six) come with some sort of bonus or ability in addition to a downside. In Danny Phantom’s case, you take less physical damage but double magic damage, and can pass through solid objects at the cost of taking on some Stress. I love transformations as a way to add further depth of your character or as a narrative plot thread, and the fact that they don’t count against any sort of domain or character limit (outside of only being allowed a single transformation at a time, but that’s what house rules are for) opens up all sorts of possibilities. Now, if Darrington Press could just make an official Super Sentai / Power Ranger transformation equivalent, I’d be all set! Castle High already features teenagers with attitude as the player characters, after all. Daggerheart: Hope & Fear is a good first expansion, though it feels like a safe one. It adds a fair amount of new content for both players and GMs to mess around with, which is always great, even if some additions feel like they should have been included from the start. The Dread domain and how it can mess with the GM’s plans directly is a really fun twist. I’ve already gushed about the transformations, and I can’t wait to see what new options get added down the road. That all said, since it launched, Daggerheart feels like a game that is far more intimidating to play for those who aren’t comfortable with improvisation and narrating what they are doing, and Hope & Fear doesn’t really help with that. I enjoy what it adds, but if you were already overwhelmed by the core game, don’t look to this expansion to save you. Daggerheart as a system is still, comparatively, in its infancy, and I would love to see a well-put-together starter kit or more hand-holdy expansion to help new players get into things.
items.title_en: Daggerheart: Hope & Fear Expansion Review

items.title: When GTA 5 Took On Zuckerberg and Hit Peak Satire
items.excerpt: This is how Rockstar brought together bad fashion, a miserable gangster, an exploding phone, and fake Zuckerberg getting his just deserts to create GTA 5's memorable takedown of Silicon Valley.
items.content_text: There’s a lot of shooting and driving in Grand Theft Auto missions, they’re kind of your main verbs in the game. You drive, shoot, and drive some more with the possibility of shooting again. They’re not very dynamic as a wireframe, so it’s a good thing that Rockstar leads the industry in storytelling, character, and satire. Missions burst with thematic meaning, every second an opportunity to push someone forward or revel in gags. It doesn’t really matter what you do. In GTA, a mission that largely consists of buying cargo shorts against your will can rival casino heists, mid-air hijackings, and all-out urban warfare. Friend Request is an early storyline mission in Grand Theft Auto V. Tutorials are behind us but Trevor has yet to join the team. Retired crook Michael De Santa is in deep trouble, so he turns to his old accomplice Lester for help. The free-as-in-speech-not-as-in-beer software enthusiast seems willing to set up a new job, but first he needs Michael to blow open the walled garden that is Jay Norris’s skull. The CEO of LifeInvader, a clear stand-in for Facebook, is about to unveil his new surveillance nightmare: a prototype smartphone designed to “dock” with every single aspect of your existence. It’s one intrusion too far for a reclusive crank like Lester, so he tasks us with sabotaging it in a mission so linear it makes Marvel’s Wolverine look like Morrowind. Part 1: What You Do Not a whole lot! Many GTA missions stray from the shoot-em-up template, exploring the mundanity of the contemporary life that Rockstar aims to emulate. Some of our fondest GTA memories involve doing yoga and winning danceoffs, but Friend Request is uneventful even by those standards. Your first task is to go shopping, swinging by the ersatz Urban Outfitters for some techy threads. Rockstar’s reputation for railroaded, handholdy missions is notorious and not entirely unearned, and here it’s at its most egregious. During the short trip to SubUrban, Michael is free to shoot guns and cause trouble despite the hefty Jansport slung jauntily over his shoulder. You’ll have to lose your wanted level to continue, which is reasonable enough. Your options dwindle as soon as you enter the store. You must buy a vest and shorts. Choose a festive Aloha shirt or a comfy flannel and the shopkeeper will bar your progression and roast you with a frankly unwarranted “what are those?” Once you’re in disguise, you can equip guns but can’t fire them without triggering a failure state. You can approach the LifeInvader office, but the front door won’t open, and trying to blow your way in will force a restart. Drop a sticky bomb and its fission mailed before it even hits the ground. Closing pop-ups is probably the most “gameplay” in Friend Request, if you consider clicking to be ludologically satisfying. You have to pose as an IT temp, share a cig with this guy Rickie, and follow the overpaid programmer through the open plan office. You’ve now lost the ability to sprint, and besides an unlocked basement, all of the conference rooms with cutesy names are inaccessible. You can only observe until it’s time to close some pop-ups. This is probably the most “gameplay” in Friend Request, if you consider clicking to be ludologically satisfying, and even here you’re limited. You can’t click any of the websites, not that you’d want to, you sicko, nor can you open any of the enticing folders and hard drives that are just sitting on the desktop begging to be file-explored. Once you clean up Rickie's infested computer you can access the LifeInvader phone prototype in an unguarded room. There’s no need to be sneaky, no one can see you and there’s literally nothing you can do to draw their attention as you fit the device with a miniature explosive. Once the job is done, you have no option but to politely leave. You can’t play the arcade games, avail yourself of productivity-enhancing snacks, or even follow this guy into his job interview. He’ll just wait there, clutching his resume, “#OpenToWork” eternally circling his LinkedIn profile years before the green frame of shame was invented. Time to go home. You still can’t shoot, though you can use your fists and engage in enough vehicular carnage to earn a police response. Once you arrive, you must kick Tracey off the couch and tune in to Jay Norris, live from the Vinewood Bowl. While the wunderkind tech giant preaches to a choir of sycophantic fans, Michael places a call to the sabotaged smartphone and blasts Norris’s head off. You can choose not to hit send, but if you miss the mark the event is over in seconds and you fail the mission. There isn’t even any amusing dillydallying in the scene to reward your curiosity. Either hit the mission complete button or don’t. Do it in eight and a half minutes for a gold medal. On paper, it’s the opposite of exciting. You go shopping and go to work. It’s not hard to imagine how Agent 47 would have handled the whole ordeal, infiltrating the glass-walled workplace and inserting himself into all kinds of startup office drama amidst a clockwork Hitman level. The end result would have been the same though, so maybe it wouldn’t have mattered how we got there. The important stuff is what you see on the way. Part 2: What You See Within the sandbox of GTA’s open worlds are palaces purpose-built for spectacular cinematic setpieces. A suspiciously detailed museum, or a motel with chest-high walls, maybe. Busy seaports and concrete canals. These bespoke and intentional spaces exist to demonstrate Rockstar’s technical mastery and excellence in encounter design. The folks in Edinburgh like to flex their muscles, and a mission like Friend Request is just a different way of showing off. It’s the signature satirical moment of GTA 5, a provocative piss-take ripped from the headlines as well as from the third-best Gerard Butler movie. Friend Request is a showcase for Rockstar’s edgy bravado packed into a bite-sized breather mission with more jokes-per-minute than a whole season of 30 Rock. If Rockstar’s railroading has an upside, it’s making sure the stuff they’re forcing you to see is highly-concentrated entertainment in bulk. With our hand fully in the designer’s grasp, we’re led through a slice of life diorama dense with gags and observations, like an EPCOT exhibit that transports us to the early 2010s. It was a time of economic exuberance, when a couple of` guys with a crazy dream could open a restaurant where appetizers are called “shareables.” Tech startups emerged aggressively as the iPhone revolution took hold, with low interest rates enabling lavish offsites and office perks like matcha on tap and unlimited fig bars. LifeInvader’s workplace obsession with air guitar echoes entire Agile squads doing the Harlem Shake, all for the Vine. Friend Request captures this earnest arrogance with a field researcher’s eye, no doubt informed by the observations of Rockstar creatives throughout their global network of office spaces where they spent a lot of time. Whiteboards are plastered with mission statements and sprint roadmaps, while the workers in conformist techvests and khakis engage in mindless chatter and awkward standup meetings. It’s a cathartic experience for anyone who’s ever had to book a pod via a glitchy tablet or wait for the water cooler to complete a firmware update. We didn’t know how good we had it. Any “modern” satire risks aging immediately upon release. Games take a long time to make, and the targets of their pointed barbs might be old news by the time anyone gets to play them, forgotten like Foursquare and Klout. The tech industry is different now. We’re still very much living in the surveillance economy Friend Request predicted, our anxieties around social media exacerbated by glasses that record our every move. It traded bright and beachy millennial optimism for apocalyptic AI-pilled doom, with cold-pressed kombucha replaced by nicotine pouches and black market peptides. The Jay Norris of our current hellscape wouldn’t be wearing a “gillet,” whatever that is, but instead rocking a dainty chain and a $3,000 t-shirt that’s too big. His rhetoric, however, probably wouldn’t change all that much. American culture has been stuck in a rut for a while. You could travel back in time to 2013 wearing exactly what you are now and no one would bat an eye, though they probably won’t believe your warning about the Costco Guys. The memes might be different and the pivot to video is vertical, but otherwise we’re still very much living in the surveillance economy Friend Request predicted, our anxieties around social media and privacy exacerbated even more by glasses that record our every move and ugly pendants that are always listening. Rockstar’s world is no longer the one outside your window, but it’s illustrative of how we got here. Its problems seem quaint in comparison, when corporations still had to earn your phone addiction and were more interested in selling your private info than building data centers in your backyard. Friend Request almost makes you miss the good old days, a feeling with which Michael De Santa is painfully familiar. Part 3: What It Means Michael is chopped. Michael is unc. Michael is miserable. After faking his death in the disastrous North Yankton job, the master criminal is “angrily decomposing” in his stately Los Santos manor, trapped in a world he never made with a family who doesn’t respect him. This is supposed to be the good life, a cushy retirement earned from years of risk and hard work, but Michael has never felt more hollow. If the surface goal of Friend Request was to mock trends in tech and social media, the mission’s underlying purpose is to highlight Michael’s obsolescence, and in true Rockstar fashion, it’s not exactly subtle about it. Nearly every line of dialogue is a surgical strike on Michael’s self-worth. He practically begs Lester to spin up a classic guns and ski-masks heist for old-time’s sake, only to be shot down in favor of sophisticated corporate espionage. He’s forced to buy lame clothes he doesn’t understand and suffers the shopgirl’s scornful side-eye. The fresh-faced peons at LifeInvader waiting for their shares to vest barely even register the middle-aged technician in their midst, even though they’re helpless to fix their computers without his expert clicking skills. The dialogue makes the theme plain, but the lack of gameplay agency within the mission, while a Rockstar trope, also feeds the theme of Michael’s sense of inadequacy. Friend Request is built to shrink Michael, to heighten his midlife crisis and draw a contrast between the ambitious young Franklin and the unrepentant Trevor. He can’t sprint, shoot, or cause any overt trouble. He must play by this new society’s rules while gritting his teeth through the humiliation rituals of a future that’s left him behind. Call Lester after leaving LifeInvader and the mastermind brags about his K/D/R in a violent shooter. Michael brushes it off, revealing his fondness for dusty Vinewood cinema instead, but it still stings a little. The man who sent us on the quest gets to actually have fun playing a video game while Michael is on a much-derided walk and follow mission, maybe the most hated archetype outside of escorting NPCs. Way to twist the knife! The only catharsis for Michael comes at the very end of Friend Request, when his big man-of-action moment is reduced to pressing a button on his smartphone. The power in that single tap seems to rattle Michael, and the result of his fateful phone call reverberates throughout the game. LifeInvader stock plummets and never recovers, while a slate of optional assassinations allows players to further manipulate the economy and outright break it in their favor. Friend Request is the first step toward making money a complete non-issue in GTA V, and it's still not as satisfying as cracking open a vault and making a run for it. That will come soon enough. It can be cope to defend something as intentionally boring, but it’s pretty clearly the case here. Missions that top the tier list feel like blockbuster action movies, but for every Die Hard there’s a delicious dull My Dinner With Andre. GTA’s legendary, long campaigns demand frequent changes of pace, and cooldown character studies like Friend Request offer exploration of a different kind than open-world adventure. Trekking through trauma, wandering through wounded pride, we’re given space to dig beneath the skin of the people we embody and understand what drives them.
items.title_en: When GTA 5 Took On Zuckerberg and Hit Peak Satire

items.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
items.excerpt: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
items.content_text: Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow. If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power , you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch. During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants. Theo, last seen as a hopeful child of the Southlands and friend of hero elf Arondir, is now older and full of hate after five years of Númenórean oppression. Sauron sees something in him, something special, and offers Theo a gift. In Episode 2, appropriately called The Gift of Men, Sauron performs a dark ritual that lets Theo “meet” his mysterious father, or at least that’s what we think is happening here (with Sauron, you never really know!). This is a callback to a scene in Season 1 where a young Theo encounters The Hilt, a broken sword-hilt forged during the First Age. It had been left hidden in a barn where Theo discovers it, and we see Theo’s blood drip into the Hilt, somehow feeding its regeneration. Clearly, Theo had some dark power inside him, although it was left unaddressed, sparking many fan theories over recent years. In Season 3, Sauron notices the dark mark left on Theo’s arm after his interaction with The Hilt and immediately raises an eyebrow. Who was Theo’s father, really? During the ritual, Sauron uses the power of necromancy to communicate with the dead in the Unseen World. Sauron listens to the words of the dead, and tells Theo his father was named Fäldred, Son of Hammethreg. Theo asks, “Who are you, father?” The response, in Black Speech, is “Gorthmundur.” Sauron tells Theo this was a “Noble House of old, the sworn stewards of Mordor blessed with… certain powers.” These powers, it seems, were passed down to Theo. “There is a reason you were drawn to that hilt, and it to you,” Sauron continues, before suggesting that Theo might have become ruler of the Southlands had his mother not “hidden the truth.” Theo responds to say his mother told him his father left. Sauron disputes this, before issuing a revelation that sends Theo spiralling: his mother murdered his father over what he had become. Sauron, ever the opportunist, offers Theo a Ring of Power. He tells him that he has the power within him to become “a conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.” The downcast Theo accepts the gift. Fast forward to Episode 4, and one of two shock deaths that punctuate this first block of The Rings of Power Season 3. Theo, now in full Nazgnagôl gear and spurred on by Sauron, murders his friend Arondir during the escape from Gundabad. It’s a shocking twist that cements Theo’s descent into darkness, and marks the end of the road for one of the mighty heroes of The Rings of Power. In the interview below, I ask Tyroe Muhafidin about Theo’s journey in these first four episodes, what it’s like to play a Nazgnagôl, and where the murder of Arondir leaves The Rings of Power. And yes, we get into the question of Theo’s parentage. Was Sauron telling him the truth about his father? IGN: The first question is an obvious one: how does it feel to be playing a Nazgnagôl? Tyroe Muhafidin: It was crazy. The costume automatically gives you a sense of such great strength and power. The biggest thing for me was, as soon as I put on those gauntlets there was an automatic transforming moment for me where you could just feel the power through your body. And it's interesting because I went from playing basically a helpless child to some godlike being. So it was a real jump and I had to do a lot of work in terms of my physicality and trying to look powerful and strong, which was something so new to me because I've always been scrawny and helpless. So yeah, it was a challenge, but I think I got there in the end, and I'm super, super grateful that I've got a chance to be something so iconic and to play something so iconic. IGN: What is your understanding of what Nazgnagôl are, as it was explained to you? Tyroe Muhafidin: So a Nazgûl directly translates to Ringwraith, whereas Nazgnagôl directly translates to Ring Servant. At this point in time when we've just put the ring on, we're not quite wraiths yet. We are still human men with autonomy over their body and can make their own decisions. We're just a lot stronger now. We've got a lot of power and a lot of dark power. An important thing to know is at the beginning of this season, the One Ring hasn't yet been made. So these rings are yet to be binded completely to Sauron's will, where we are not now complete, I guess, his minions. We still have autonomy over who we are. That was the fun thing to play in this season, the gradual descent into more and more madness and more and more evil and darkness. But at this point in time, we get to very much still be people, just very strong people, I guess. IGN: There's a really interesting scene where Sauron reveals Theo's parentage to him. What's your understanding of who Theo's father is? Sauron is suggesting at that moment that Theo has an innate power as a result of his parentage, but it's left ambiguous. And Sauron looks emotional even as he's talking to Theo about this. I almost was thinking he almost looks at him as his own son in some ways. So what's your read on that? What can you tell us about what all that means? Tyroe Muhafidin: It's revealed that his father was the head of a few dark sorcerers and he sided with the dark side a long time ago, alongside his peers and the other Southlanders who sided with Sauron. And so there's that kind of information that's brought out. But I think the big thing for Theo is when Sauron says his mother killed him when she found out. And I think that moment for me, and I think for Theo as a whole, it kind of sends a spin in the works of, what is Sauron really doing here and what is he trying to accomplish? Is he just trying to say words to make Theo happy, trying to build this broken boy up? Because he can see something for sure. And I don't think Theo really realizes. But I think there was always a dark side to Theo and maybe it was inherited, but that relationship to the Hilt was always something that stuck with him. And I think maybe when he got a taste of that darkness in the Hilt, maybe it was the first time he kind of felt the presence of his father, and maybe that's why it was so addictive, that feeling to him. So I think this season we find out a little bit more of where he comes from. But I think the biggest thing is, how much of it is the truth? What is Sauron saying that is manipulation and deceit and what is the truth? Which I think is kind of the fun dynamic of those scenes, is you feel like you're finding out a lot, but are you really? IGN: There is a big moment in Episode 4 where Theo kills Arondir, a character who's been in the series from the beginning. When you first found out you'd be doing that, what was your reaction? Tyroe Muhafidin: It was interesting. I was excited because I was like, "Oh, this is some juicy stuff to get into." But I think the moment I got the script, I found out and I was really excited because it was going to be some really cool stuff. When I read it all, it all became very real for me. And it was like, "Wow, this is a big task. This is super daunting." And there were months of intense anxiety coming up to this moment. But yeah, I guess I was just super excited, but anxious at the same time. And I feel like I knew at some point something big like this was going to happen. So I think it was just a matter of being prepared for it and trying to service Ismail [Cruz Córdova, who plays Arondir] as well, the best I possibly could. IGN: What do you think the character death means for the show at that point and the story it's telling, but also for Theo? Do you see it as this is a moment that we see a tipping point in him that the audience is like, "Okay, yes, he has really gone too far." Tyroe Muhafidin: In terms of the show, it's a moment of no-one is safe and there's no mercy from the dark side. And this war is very much real. The most talented and bravest of your warriors will go down. And that's kind of, I think, setting the premise for the rest of the war that's going to go on. I think for Theo specifically, it definitely was that tipping point where his decision is made and his destiny is decided. And I think he realizes this afterwards as well, and whether he agrees with that decision he's made or not, he's made that decision. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 episodes 1-4 are out now on Prime Video. Check back with IGN after Episodes 5 and 6 are released this week for more.

items.title: James Gunn Shuts Down Rumors That Skydance Is Meddling With Man of Tomorrow
items.excerpt: James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.
items.content_text: James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit . The internet has filled with gossip in the wake of Gunn and Peter Safran's departure as co-chairmen of the comic book entertainment wing earlier this week. As an ocean of rumors rises, some of the more worrying claims have seen some suggest Skydance has already taken control of the Superman director's sequel, which could result in major characters like Supergirl and Blue Beetle being cut entirely. These are just some of the accusations that Gunn sought to dispel in a Threads post tonight. In what is essentially his first public statement since leaving DC Studios, the filmmaker took aim at the gossip that has DCU fans concerned. Not only have "sweeping changes" to Man of Tomorrow not been made, but apparently, no one at Skydance has even seen his movie yet. "There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen Man of Tomorrow and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made," he said. "No one from Skydance has even seen the movie - the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false." It's a response that will not answer every question comic book movie enjoyers have about the future of the DCU, but it does clear the air about much of the more damning chatter online. Gunn's comments mean that any talk of Skydance being unhappy with the current cut of Man of Tomorrow is false. It also sounds like, at least for now, Supergirl and Blue Beetle, who had been previously reported to return, are safe. With so much time left before David Corenswet's Clark Kent returns to theaters in July, though, it's hard to say how the Skydance takeover may impact its release. It's best to wait until Gunn or Skydance has more to share before setting any firm expectations in place for now. All of that said, it's not too hard to see why fans of the DCU have felt uneasy in the last few days. Gunn and Safran have orchestrated the DCU to tell a varied collection of superpowered stories for four years, with its overarching plan for the years ahead only just starting to come into view. Pulling them from the driver's seat means the future is more unknown than ever before, especially considering Skydance was quick to find a replacement in Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham. Will Man of Tomorrow be altered against Gunn's will? Will Skydance reboot the DC movie universe and scrap future plans for the DCU? How will any of this affect future entries in Robert Pattinson's The Batman saga? It's all too soon to tell, but that won't stop the rumor mill from pushing ahead. What we do know is what Gunn shared with fans in the immediate aftermath of his exit. In a letter posted to social media , he promised that the characters he and Safran helped set up "will live on." He also confirmed that the duo was recently "engaged on another DC project" that he is writing. What that project is remains a mystery. For more on the future of the DCU, you can read up on what we know about Latcham . You can also check out another report that suggested Skydance intends to prioritize more well-known heroes in the DC portfolio going forward . Man of Tomorrow, meanwhile, is set to premiere July 9, 2027. Photo by Michael Kovac/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Pictures.

items.title: After Another Year of Price Hikes, What Streaming Deals Will We Get for Black Friday 2026?
items.content_text: We’re officially in the thick of deals season, and if there’s one thing I personally spend way too much money on, it’s streaming subscriptions. It doesn't help that everyone keeps hiking prices, and deals are rarer than ever. Thankfully, there’s one time of year where you can often get a decent amount of those very subscriptions for much cheaper than usual: Black Friday . Almost every service is likely to drop some type of deal, though the majority will be on ad-supported plans. If you’ve been intrigued by any particular service, or want to strategize some free trials and cancellations, here’s what streaming deals I expect we’ll see for Black Friday this year. Black Friday Streaming Deal Predictions In general, deals will certainly be live from Black Friday (November 27) to Cyber Monday (November 30). However, some services may launch their Black Friday deals in the week before the main event. Amazon Prime Video Starting from the top, obviously Amazon will be all over Black Friday (check out the retailer’s full sale schedule). Prime Video is included in Amazon memberships, which pretty much never go on sale. The service does offer a 30-day free trial and a hefty 50% discount for anyone under the age of 25. Channel Add-Ons, however, like AMC+ and Britbox, will likely have deals through Prime Video in addition to their own platforms. Amazon’s general Black Friday sale starts November 19, but I imagine most Add-On discounts will appear on Black Friday proper. Disney+ and Hulu Disney+ has always launched some sort of Black Friday deal, but as we’ve seen across streaming, the discounts have gotten less generous over time. Last year , Black Friday came right after Disney+ rolled out a price hike. The Black Friday deal only applied to the ad-supported bundle of both services, dropping the monthly price from $12.99 to $4.99 for a full 12 months. Disney+ increased prices again back in September , but the Hulu bundle actually stayed at $12.99. I’d guess we see the return of the $4.99 deal on the ad-supported bundle for a full 12-month window, but there’s a chance it only goes down to $5.99 to align with the new Disney+ pricing. HBO Max HBO Max is in a particularly weird place. Paramount finalized its acquisition of Warner Bros. earlier this year, and indicated early on in negotiations they were planning to merge their streaming services . More recently, Paramount announced that HBO Max and Paramount+ will be getting a new streaming bundle in early 2027 , which is likely a first step on the path to a full merger. However, that doesn’t mean Black Friday deals are off the table. Last year , HBO Max offered a particularly generous deal, dropping the ad-supported plan to just $2.99/month for a 12-month period. We’ll likely see the same deal return this year, though potentially limited to six or even two months as HBO Max navigates a more uncertain future. Paramount+ Paramount+ is in a similar boat to HBO Max, but I’m a bit more confident in this one, largely because Paramount+ has offered relatively consistent deals even as other services have shied away from them. Right now, for example, you can get 50% off an annual subscription using a promo code . For Black Friday, Paramount+ will likely offer a two-month subscription deal on both of its ad-supported and ad-free Showtime plans. Yep, we might actually have an ad-free deal on our hands. In 2025 , Paramount+ dropped the prices of both subscriptions to $2.99/month, and given the consistency of deals since then, I expect to see the same deal return for 2026. Apple TV Speaking of ad-free, praise be Apple TV. Apple’s streaming service keeps it simple with one ad-free subscription plan, so if you’re dead set on picking up a new service without ads, this is your best bet. Last year , Apple TV dropped the price of its subscription from $12.99 to $5.99/month for a six-month period. Since then, however, the service hiked prices by $2 for a standard monthly rate of $14.99. With that in mind, I expect to see the return of at least a six-month deal period, but the discount might be closer to $6.99 to hit the same discount percentage. Peacock Peacock was actually one of the only streaming services that didn’t offer any Black Friday deal in 2025. That doesn’t mean we’re out of luck this year, but it isn’t a great sign, especially given the service just hiked prices again this Summer. If you desperately want to catch up on Peacock’s sitcoms and reality TV lineup, I recommend keeping an eye out for deals on Walmart+ subscriptions . This is basically Walmart’s version of Amazon Prime, but it also includes Peacock Premium , and often get 50% discounts during major sales events.
